summary: Defines a new attribute type and an auxiliary object class to store URIs, including URLs, in directory entries in a standard way.

eli5.summary: A phone book entry gets a new line for a web address. This note says how to write it down.

questions: how to store urls in an x.500 directory
how to store a url in an ldap entry
subtitle: A standard way to store web addresses, with optional labels, in LDAP and X.500 directory entries.

tldr.problem: URLs were widely used and groups were already putting them in LDAP and X.500 directories, each in their own way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the multivalued labeledURI attribute and an auxiliary object class, labeledURIObject, so any URI can be stored with an optional human-readable label.
tldr.outcome: Directory entries can carry URIs in a common form. An earlier labeledURL attribute is deprecated.

today: RFC 2079 is a Proposed Standard, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Background and Intended Use
sections.content:
URLs, as defined in RFC 1738, are the first of several kinds of Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs). Several groups were already experimenting with putting URLs in LDAP and X.500 directories. This RFC builds on that work and defines an X.500 attribute type called labeledURI and an auxiliary object class called labeledURIObject.

They are designed for LDAP and X.500 directories and may be used elsewhere.
sections.eli5: People wanted to put web addresses into directories, so this note picks one common way to do it.

sections.title: The labeledURI Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute has the caseExactString syntax, because URIs are case-sensitive, and it is multivalued. Its OID is 1.3.6.1.4.1.250.1.57. A value is a URI (at present a URL) optionally followed by one or more spaces and a label. Spaces cannot appear unencoded in a URI, so it is clear where the label starts.

The label is a friendly name for people, and the RFC proposes no syntax for it. Non-ASCII characters in it are discouraged. If used, they should follow X.500 conventions, not HTML ones. Several values usually point to different related resources, but may be different locations for one resource.
sections.eli5: Each entry holds a web address, and after a space you can add a short note about it, like a caption.

sections.title: Object Class and Examples
sections.content:
The labeledURIObject class (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.250.3.15) is a subclass of top that may contain labeledURI. It can be added to existing directory objects. The attribute can also be placed directly in other object classes.

Examples include http://www.umich.edu/%7Ersug/ldap/ LDAP Home Page, with the label "LDAP Home Page", and http://champagne.inria.fr/Unites/rennes.gif Rennes [photo], where the label hints the target is a photo.
sections.eli5: The object class is a sticker you can put on an existing directory entry to give it a place for web addresses.

sections.title: Security and the Deprecated labeledURL
sections.content:
The memo says security is not discussed, except to warn that blindly inserting a label into an HTML document is not recommended. A malicious label could carry HTML tags that mislead viewers.

An earlier draft defined a separate labeledURL attribute. It is deprecated and should not be used for new values, because the IETF-ASID working group decided one attribute is better than two. Clients may support it to ease the transition.
sections.eli5: Do not paste the note text into a web page without care, since a sneaky note could trick people. An old second attribute was dropped.
